native_test_cmd: python3 -m pytest tests/ops/mapper/test_text_chunk_mapper.py -q -k "not tokenizer and not dashscope and not all_text"
workload: One 302KB paragraph-broken article chunked at max_len 1000 on blank lines, the training-text path that sets both max_len and split_pattern.
notes: Each recursive call copies the unconsumed suffix and keeps that copy alive on the stack, so traced peak memory was 59MB for a 302KB article (387 chunks). An index walk over the original string produced the same chunks and does not retain those suffixes. Open upstream PRs do not edit this function.

workload: One 175KB space-tokenized document, 5-word shingles, 256 permutations, 20 bands (the default space MinHash path).
notes: compute_hash keeps a Python set of every unique joined shingle before sha1. Duplicate shingles do not change the MinHash minimum, so hashing windows without retaining those strings keeps the band bytes. On a document of the same shape the traced peak fell from about 29MB to about 1.4MB and the band hashes matched. Open upstream PRs edit document_simhash_deduplicator, not this function.

workload: One 8.3MB document of prose lines plus occasional tab fields, split with newlines and tabs enabled (get_words_from_document's hot path).
notes: Every call compiles a regex split and then drops empty pieces. Mapping newlines and tabs to spaces and using str.split returns the same tokens; that rewrite was about 4x faster on a shorter document of the same shape. Open PR 1169 edits words_refinement in this file and does not change split_on_whitespace.

workload: A batch of 24 synthetic arXiv-style papers, each with 70 newline macros (newcommand and def) and 4000 uses in the body.
notes: Each macro runs its own full-document regex substitution, so cost grows with the macro count. One alternation of the same names produced identical text on an 80-macro article and was about 4x faster (14ms vs 3.4ms). No open upstream PR edits this mapper.
